posts.title: Fall Roof Maintenance: 5 Things to Check Before Winter
posts.excerpt: Fall is the best time to prepare your roof for winter storms. Here are the five things you need to check now to avoid expensive repairs later.
posts.author: Scott Karraker
posts.content:
Why Fall Maintenance Matters

Winter in East Texas might not mean snow, but it means ice, wind, and water damage. By October, storms have already beaten up a lot of roofs, and if you don't catch the damage now, you're looking at leaks, rot, and costly repairs come January.

I always tell my customers: fix it in the fall, or pay for it in the winter. It's that simple.

The 5 Things to Check

1. Shingles and Flashing

Walk around your roof (or have someone do it for you). Look for:

  • Missing or damaged shingles—even one is a problem
  • Curled or cracked shingles
  • Flashing that's loose or separated from the roof (around vents, chimneys, skylights)

Flashing is where most leaks start. If it's not sealed tight, water will find its way in.

2. Gutters and Downspouts

Clean out your gutters. I mean really clean them. Leaves and debris clog gutters, water backs up, and next thing you know you've got water in the attic or under the siding.

While you're at it, check that downspouts are directing water at least 4-6 feet away from your foundation.

3. Roof Valleys

The valleys are where two roof planes meet—they're the highways for water running off your roof. Make sure they're clear of leaves and debris. If water gets blocked there, it has nowhere to go but into your house.

4. Vents and Penetrations

Every time something pokes through your roof—a vent pipe, an antenna, a skylight—that's a potential leak point. Check:

  • Rubber boots around vent pipes (they dry out and crack)
  • Caulk around flashing is still intact
  • No gaps or separations

5. The Attic

Go up there with a flashlight. Look for:

  • Water stains on the wood
  • Mold or mildew (dark spots on rafters)
  • Daylight coming through (if you can see light, water can get in)

The attic tells you everything. If there are stains up there, the damage started weeks or months ago.

What to Do If You Find Problems

Small repairs now are cheap. Big repairs after water damage is not.

If you find damaged shingles, loose flashing, or any signs of water, call us for an inspection. Most fall repairs take a day or two and cost way less than waiting until you've got rotted wood and mold.

Bottom Line

Fall maintenance takes a couple of hours and can save you thousands. It's the best investment you can make in your roof.

If you want a professional to do the inspection—and honestly, I recommend it if you're not comfortable on a roof—we'll come out, walk it with you, and tell you exactly what needs fixing.

Don't wait. Winter's coming.

posts.title: Why Your Insurance Adjuster Might Be Lowballing You
posts.excerpt: Your insurance adjuster doesn't work for you—they work for the insurance company. Here's how to protect yourself and maximize your claim.
posts.author: Scott Karraker
posts.content:
The Real Problem With Insurance Adjusters

I've been doing roofing in East Texas for over 15 years, and I've seen this same pattern hundreds of times: A storm hits. Hail tears up a roof. The homeowner calls their insurance company. An adjuster shows up, spends 20 minutes looking at the damage, and tells them what they'll pay.

Most of the time, that number is wrong.

The adjuster either misses damage—sometimes intentionally. Or they lowball you because the faster they close the claim, the better it looks for their company. I've had customers get told their roof damage is $3,000 when the actual replacement cost is $12,000 to $18,000. That's not an accident. It's how the game is played.

Why This Happens

Insurance adjusters work for the insurance company, not for you. I know that sounds obvious, but a lot of people don't really understand what that means. It means:

  • They're incentivized to pay out less. The company's profit depends on it.
  • They're rushed. They're handling dozens of claims. Yours gets 20 minutes of their time.
  • They're not roofers. A lot of adjusters don't know what they're looking at. They follow a checklist and move on.

How to Protect Yourself

Here's what I do for my customers, and here's what you should do if you have storm damage:

1. Get a Professional Inspection Before the Adjuster

Don't wait for the insurance company. Call a licensed roofing contractor—like us—and get a detailed inspection. We take photos. We document the damage. We measure the roof. We write it all down.

This gives you proof of what's actually wrong, and it gives you leverage when the adjuster shows up.

2. Be There When the Adjuster Inspects

Don't let them look at your roof alone. Be present. Take notes. Ask questions. Better yet, have your roofer there too.

An adjuster who knows a licensed roofer is standing there watching them is going to be more thorough. They know they can't skip details.

3. Don't Accept the First Number

If the adjuster's estimate doesn't match your roofer's inspection, push back. Ask for an explanation. Provide the documentation you have. If they still won't budge, request a re-inspection or ask about the appeal process.

What Reliable Roofing Does

When a customer has storm damage, here's our process:

  1. Free damage inspection. We come out, look at everything, take photos, and give you a detailed assessment.
  2. We meet with the adjuster on-site. I'm there with you. I know what to look for. I know what insurance will try to skip over. And I know the work better than anyone.
  3. We handle the paperwork. We work with the insurance company to make sure the claim reflects the real damage.
  4. Claim approved—we complete the work. Once it's covered, we do the job right.

This changes the conversation. Most of the time, we end up with a claim that actually covers the real damage.

Bottom Line

Your insurance adjuster is not your friend. They're doing their job, which is to minimize what the insurance company pays out. You need to protect yourself.

That means getting a professional inspection, being present during the adjuster's visit, and not settling for the first number they throw at you.

If you've had storm damage—hail, wind, lightning, whatever—call us for a free inspection. No pressure. We'll look at it, tell you what we see, and if you want us there when the adjuster shows up, we will be.

That's what Reliable Roofing does.
